name: DoS attack construction and countermeasure/responsibility analysis
identify_givens: A request-response or publish-subscribe service/protocol described message by message, usually over UDP with spoofable source IP addresses and weak or missing source authentication (no MAC/signature over the whole message, or a check that only covers part of the message). An attacker model is stated: attacker has less bandwidth than the victim, may eavesdrop/intercept traffic, but cannot recover keys. Sometimes a named flood (SYN/ICMP) or a service whose work-per-request is expensive or whose replies are much larger than requests.
identify_target: Describe concretely how the attacker performs a DoS of a stated victim (server or a client) despite having less bandwidth; then describe how the vulnerability can be countered (and, when asked, who must deploy the countermeasure: attacker's ISP, the service, or the cloud provider).
identify_keywords: describe how this vulnerability can be countered
strategy_name: Exploit spoofing + asymmetry (amplification or state exhaustion), then authenticate the source

algorithm.detail: List each protocol message, its transport (UDP = spoofable source IP, TCP = handshake-verified source), and what work or traffic each message triggers at the server (replies, stored state, downstream messages to third parties).

Check what actually authenticates the sender: an unauthenticated UDP source IP can be forged; a field that is encrypted/checked separately from the rest of the message (e.g. only $X = E(IP_i, K_i)$ is verified while $L$ travels in plaintext) can be tampered with by a man in the middle.

Spot the amplification factor (one small request triggers many/large replies, e.g. $L$ bytes split into 512 KB blocks, or one publish triggers a message per subscriber per topic) or the exhaustion target (server memory/connection table grows per forged subscription or half-open SYN).

Combine the gap and the asymmetry: spoof the victim's IP (or intercept and tamper the unprotected field, e.g. raise $L$) so the server either floods the victim with amplified traffic, or is itself exhausted by mass forged requests. State why 'less bandwidth' does not matter: the server supplies the bandwidth.

Authenticate the whole message and verify the source before committing resources: use TCP (handshake proves the source address) or sign/MAC/encrypt the entire message, e.g. $E(IP_i \,\|\, L, K_i)$ so tampering $L$ is detected; add a nonce/sequence number/expiration against replay; add rate limiting.

If asked who deploys what: spoofing is fixed at the source by the attacker's ISP via ingress/egress filtering (BCP 38); victim-side filtering fails because the upstream link is already congested; the service fixes its own authentication and resource-commitment logic.

variations.name: Tampering instead of spoofing
variations.detail: In dasak19 P1 the protocol does authenticate the client ($D(X, K_i) = IP_i$ is checked), so pure IP spoofing fails — the trap is to overlook that $L$ is sent in plaintext: a man in the middle raises $L$ and gets amplification anyway. Adapt step 2: check which fields are inside the authenticated portion, attack the ones outside.

variations.name: Victim is the server, not a client
variations.detail: In dasak18 P1 the attacker targets the server itself: mass forged subscriptions exhaust server memory, or one forged publish forces the server to emit hundreds of messages. Adapt step 4: choose between traffic amplification against third parties and state/resource exhaustion of the server — the official solution accepts either.

variations.name: Role reversal: replay to force expensive work
variations.detail: Some sittings replace spoofing with replay: unauthenticated (or nonce-less signed) messages are re-sent to force repeated expensive server work (malware scans, many hash comparisons). The fix still follows step 5: nonce/timestamp inside the signed portion plus rate limiting.

variations.name: Named flood with responsibility question
variations.detail: 2022/NEN-style variants name the threat (SYN flood, ICMP flood, amplification via open resolvers) and ask who must act. Trap: saying the victim or its cloud provider should filter — the upstream link is already saturated, so ingress filtering (BCP 38) belongs to the attacker's ISP; SYN floods need cookies/backlog fixes at the server.

example_problem: Denial of service (dasak18, Part II Problem 1). A news feed service S lets clients subscribe to topics from content providers. Protocol (all UDP): to subscribe to topic T, client Ci sends <IPi, IPs, T> to S; to publish news, publisher Pj sends <IPj, IPs, N, T1...Tn> where N is the content and T1...Tn the topics; when news is published, S sends <IPs, IPi, D> to every client registered for at least one relevant topic. Describe how a malicious user can abuse this to DoS the server S, given the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim, and how to counter it.

example_steps.work: Flows: subscribe (client->S, stores state per client/topic), publish (publisher->S, triggers one UDP message S->Ci per subscribed client). Everything is UDP, so every source IP field can be forged.
Authentication gap: neither the subscribe nor the publish message carries any credential — S trusts the claimed source IP in a spoofable UDP datagram.

Asymmetry: one forged publish with n topics triggers up to one outbound message per registered client (amplification), and each forged subscription permanently consumes server memory (state exhaustion).

Official solution: the attacker spoofs the IPs of several clients Ci and registers them to hundreds of topics, then spoofs the IP of a publisher Pj and publishes an article with hundreds of topics, forcing the server to send hundreds of messages to several clients. Alternatively, the attacker exhausts the server's memory by continuously subscribing (forged) users.

Official countermeasure: use TCP (the handshake verifies the source address, defeating spoofing) or some sort of authentication on subscribe/publish messages, so forged registrations and publishes are rejected.
